questions.question: You are designing a multi-step Claude workflow where some steps must reason without seeing the full prior conversation history. The team wants to keep specific context isolated to specific steps. The context engineering technique you would use is...

options.text: Augmenting the context with all available content at every step so each step has access to the entire prior history of the workflow during its reasoning.
Embedding the full prior history in each step regardless of whether the step needs the prior history for its reasoning.
Using a single global prompt that applies to every step in the workflow no matter what each step is reasoning about during its run.
Context isolation through subagents or multi-step agentic workflows that scope each step's context to only what the step needs.

questions.explanation: Context has to be isolated per step, so use subagents or a multi-step workflow where each step sees only what it needs. A and B do the opposite of what is asked by stuffing in the whole history. C uses one shared prompt, which isolates nothing. Remember: context isolation = subagents / multi-step scoping.

questions.question: You are designing a Claude application that will process customer support tickets in two stages: a triage stage that classifies tickets and a response stage that drafts replies. The team is debating whether to use a single Claude call that handles both stages or separate Claude calls for each stage. How would you structure the application?

options.text: Use a single Claude call for triage and then use a non-Claude rule-based system for response generation, on the grounds that rule-based systems are more reliable for drafting replies.
Use separate Claude calls for triage and response, because each stage has distinct inputs, outputs, and success criteria that benefit from focused prompts.
Use a single Claude call for both stages, on the grounds that a single call is cheaper than multiple calls in any production Claude application setup.
Use multiple Claude calls in parallel that each draft a complete ticket reply, then have a fourth Claude call select the best one to send to the customer.

questions.explanation: The two stages have different inputs, outputs and success criteria, so split them into two calls with focused prompts. C argues that one call is always cheaper, but cost is not the deciding factor here. D builds an unnecessary multi-agent setup for a two-step problem. Remember: different goals = separate prompts/calls.

questions.question: Your Claude application has been running for several conversation turns, and you notice the model occasionally references information that was discussed many turns ago but is no longer relevant. You suspect context drift is causing the model to weight stale content too heavily. How would you address the drift?

options.text: Truncate the conversation so the model sees only the most recent turn during each subsequent response.
Reset the conversation after every turn so the model loses all prior turns when generating a response.
Apply compaction to summarize older portions of the conversation so the gist remains while the specifics carry less weight.
Increase the context window size so all turns of the conversation remain visible to the model in full detail.

questions.explanation: Context drift comes from old content kept in full detail, so use compaction: summarize the older part to keep the gist while reducing the weight of the details. A and B cut or wipe everything and lose state that is still needed. D enlarges the context window, which only keeps old content around longer. Remember: drift → compaction, not truncation or reset.

questions.question: A teammate has asked why your Claude application sometimes produces a response that includes the prompt text repeated back, and other times produces a response with the prompt text rephrased. They suspect a bug in the application's request construction. How would you respond?

options.text: Explain that LLMs generate output token by token, and variation in how prompt content appears in output is a property of generation, not a bug in request construction.
Confirm that the variation is a bug in the application's request construction and start investigating which part of the application is producing the inconsistent prompt text.
Tell the teammate that the variation depends on which Claude model serves the request, and recommend pinning the application to a single model version to make the output behavior consistent.
Tell the teammate that the variation is caused by the application sending two different prompts on different runs and propose a code change that pins the system prompt to a single version.

questions.explanation: Sequential token generation is inherent to LLMs; whether prompt content reappears verbatim or paraphrased is a property of generation, not a request-building bug. B, C and D all claim a bug or blame a different model version or prompt without any evidence. Remember: varying phrasing = nature of generation, not a bug.

questions.question: A new Claude model release includes performance improvements for several reasoning tasks but has changed the format of its responses to system prompts that use multi-section instructions. Your application uses multi- section system prompts heavily. Initial evaluation on the application's actual workload shows the new model performs 8 percent better on reasoning tasks but produces malformed output on roughly 3 percent of requests because of the format change. The team is debating whether to upgrade. How would you decide?

options.text: Adapt the application's system prompt to the new model's format expectations and reevaluate, then upgrade only if the adapted prompt eliminates the malformed output while preserving the reasoning improvements.
Upgrade and add a downstream validation step that catches the 3 percent malformed output before it reaches users, treating the validation step as the team's mitigation for the format change.
Stay on the previous model permanently to avoid the malformed output rate and any future format changes that subsequent model releases might introduce in the application.
Upgrade immediately, because the 8 percent reasoning improvement outweighs the 3 percent malformed output rate across the application's typical request distribution.

questions.explanation: The malformed output comes from a prompt that does not fit the new format, so fix the cause (adjust the prompt), re-evaluate, and upgrade only once the errors are gone and the gains are kept. B hides the symptom with downstream validation; D ignores the errors because the benefit numbers look bigger; C freezes the version permanently. Remember: version change → adapt the prompt + re-evaluate, then upgrade.

questions.question: Your Claude application makes high-volume API calls during business hours and very few calls overnight. The team is concerned about staying within rate limits during peak hours and wants to understand how the Claude API enforces those limits. How would you proceed?

options.text: Examine the peak-hour request patterns in your application logs and smooth traffic by distributing requests more evenly across the business-hours window.
Review the API documentation for streaming endpoints and evaluate whether migrating peak-hour calls to streaming reduces exposure to rate limit enforcement.
Assess the average payload size of current API calls and consolidate requests where possible to reduce the total number of calls made during peak hours.
Identify the rate limits, design the application to stay within them during peak hours, and use exponential backoff when limits are reached.

questions.explanation: Handling rate limits properly has two parts: designing to stay within the limits, and exponential backoff when a limit is hit. A, B and C are secondary optimizations (smoothing traffic, streaming, batching payloads) that never mention backoff, the core of the question. Remember: rate limits = design within limits + exponential backoff.

questions.question: You are designing a Claude application that helps medical researchers analyze multi-step clinical case studies. The application must work through differential diagnoses by considering symptom patterns, weighing evidence across competing hypotheses, and showing intermediate reasoning steps before producing a final recommendation. The team is choosing among Claude's available model options. The model option best suited to this use case is...

options.text: A smaller model with a tighter context window, which encourages the model to focus its limited capacity on the task.
Zero-shot prompting alone with no model option adjustments, which keeps the application's configuration as simple as possible.
Fast mode, which prioritizes the lowest possible latency at the expense of reasoning depth on complex tasks.
Extended thinking, which lets the model reason through the differential diagnosis steps before producing the final recommendation.

questions.explanation: The task needs to weigh several competing hypotheses and expose intermediate reasoning steps, so use extended thinking. A and C go against the requirement (shrinking capability, prioritizing latency). B is not a model option. Remember: multi-step reasoning with visible intermediate steps = extended thinking.

questions.question: You are choosing between using STDIO-based communication and HTTP-based communication for an MCP server. The server will be invoked by a Claude Code session running locally. Which communication pattern would you use?

options.text: HTTP on the grounds that HTTP is preferable to STDIO in any context the application might encounter during normal operation.
HTTP polling against the MCP server, treating HTTP as a substitute for the standard MCP communication patterns.
STDIO because STDIO is well-suited to local process communication and avoids unnecessary network setup.
STDIO and HTTP simultaneously for redundancy, with the team running two communication patterns at the same time across Claude Code sessions.

questions.explanation: The MCP server is called by a Claude Code session running locally, so use STDIO: it suits communication between local processes and needs no network setup. A uses an absolute argument ('HTTP is always better'); D runs both patterns in parallel, which is pointless complexity. Remember: local MCP = STDIO; remote or many clients = HTTP.

questions.question: You are choosing a Claude model for a high-volume classification task. Each classification is straightforward, latency requirements are tight, and per-request cost matters at scale. Which model would you choose?

options.text: A mid-tier Claude model selected by default, because mid-tier models balance quality and cost in a way the team can apply across most tasks.
Multiple Claude models in series, where each request runs through more than one model and the application combines the outputs into a final classification.
The largest, highest-capability Claude model, to maximize quality on every classification the application produces during normal operation across all requests.
A smaller, faster Claude model, because the task is straightforward and the workload prioritizes latency and per-request cost at scale.

questions.explanation: A simple task with tight latency where per-request cost matters at scale calls for a smaller, faster model. A picks by default rather than by requirements; C maximizes quality regardless of the constraints; B chaining several models multiplies cost. Remember: high-volume classification = the smallest model that meets the bar.

questions.question: Your Claude application validates structured output but has been treating validation failures as terminal errors. Each validation failure causes the entire user request to fail. The team wants to handle validation failures more gracefully. How would you handle the validation failures?

options.text: Tell users that validation failures are unavoidable and instruct them to perform manual accuracy checks before relying on outputs.
Pass validation failures directly to downstream systems and let each downstream system decide how to handle the malformed output.
Treat validation failures as a recognized error path that triggers retry, repair, or fallback logic before failing the user request.
Disable output validation until the underlying cause of validation failures has been identified and addressed in a future release.

questions.explanation: A validation failure should be a recognized error path that triggers retry, repair or fallback before the whole request is allowed to fail. D turning off validation abandons control; B pushes broken output downstream; A shifts the checking onto users. Remember: validation failure = recognized error path (retry/repair/fallback).

questions.question: You are setting up a Claude application that requires API keys for several external services. What is the best way to store the keys?

options.text: Store the keys in a secrets manager or environment-specific configuration that is not checked into source code, and load them at runtime.
Use a single shared key across all external services, so any developer working on the application can find the keys easily during development.
Email the keys to each developer as needed and have each developer paste the keys into their local environment when they begin working on the application's code.
Put the keys in the application's configuration file and check the configuration file into the team's repository alongside the rest of the source code.

questions.explanation: Secrets belong in a secrets manager or environment-specific configuration that is not committed to source code, loaded at runtime. B, C and D are three ways of leaking secrets: sharing one key, sending it by email, committing it to the repo. Remember: API keys → secrets manager / environment, loaded at runtime.

questions.question: You are running Claude Code as part of an automated continuous integration pipeline. The pipeline needs Claude Code to execute a set of well-defined tasks without prompting for confirmation, and the output needs to be captured for downstream processing. How would you configure the pipeline?

options.text: Replace Claude Code with a different tool that does not require any configuration to operate without confirmation prompts in the pipeline.
Run Claude Code in interactive mode and have a developer manually approve every confirmation prompt while the pipeline executes its tasks.
Run Claude Code in headless mode with the required permissions configured in settings.json and capture its output for downstream processing.
Disable Claude Code's confirmation prompts globally across all environments so the pipeline runs without interruption from any prompt.

questions.explanation: CI has to run non-interactively, so use headless mode, configure permissions in settings.json, and capture the output for downstream processing. D disables confirmation prompts in every environment, spreading the risk beyond CI. B puts a person into an automated loop. Remember: CI = headless mode + permissions in settings.json.

questions.question: You are reviewing an architectural diagram for a Claude-powered travel-booking system. The diagram shows a top-level component that interprets user requests and three subordinate components that handle flights, hotels, and ground transportation. The top-level component is responsible for routing each request, sequencing the subordinate components, and reconciling their outputs into a final itinerary. The diagram also shows that each subordinate component has its own tool list and own short conversation history that is not shared with the others. Which architectural pattern does this diagram most closely describe?

options.text: A pipeline pattern, where each component processes the user request in sequence and passes the full conversation history along with the request to the next component in the pipeline.
A manager and supervisor pattern with shared context, where the top-level agent and the subagents all share a single conversation history that grows as the request flows through the system.
A retrieval-augmented pattern, where the top-level component retrieves relevant context from the subordinate components' indexed data stores before generating each response.
A manager and supervisor pattern with isolated context per subagent, where the top-level agent coordinates specialized subagents that each maintain their own conversation history and tool list.

questions.explanation: One higher-level component coordinating several specialized subagents, each with its own tool list and unshared history, is a manager/supervisor pattern with isolated context. B differs in exactly one detail: 'shared context'. The question says history is not shared, so it is out. Always read the distinguishing clause carefully. Remember: coordination + per-subagent history = supervisor with isolated context.

questions.question: A teammate is debugging a Claude application whose system prompt has grown to several hundred lines and now contains overlapping, contradictory, and obsolete instructions. How would you advise the teammate?

options.text: Audit the prompt for overlap, contradiction, and obsolete content, then refactor so each instruction is clear, current, and non-redundant.
Tighten only the contradictory rules first, treating the overlap and obsolete content as lower-priority work the team can address later.
Split the prompt across multiple system prompts so the model sees a smaller portion at any given time.
Add more explicit instructions so the most recent rules dominate the model's interpretation of the prompt during each request.

questions.explanation: A bloated prompt with duplicated, conflicting and outdated instructions needs an audit and a refactor so each instruction is clear, current and not redundant. B fixes only part of it; C splitting the prompt does not resolve the conflicts; D adds instructions to override old ones, making the prompt messier. Remember: bloated prompt = audit + refactor, not more layers.

questions.question: You are designing an agent that processes vendor invoices. The work involves a small number of well- understood steps, but occasionally an invoice arrives in an unexpected format that requires the system to decide between rerouting, requesting clarification, or flagging for human review. The most appropriate architecture for this system is...

options.text: A workflow for the standard path with an agent invoked at the decision point for unexpected formats.
A manager agent that delegates each step of standard invoice processing to a dedicated subagent, with a separate subagent handling each unexpected format.
A single large prompt that processes every incoming invoice, both standard and unexpected, in one model call.
A fully autonomous agent that handles every invoice from start to finish across all formats.

questions.explanation: The main path consists of well-understood steps, so it is a workflow; an agent is called only at the point that needs judgment (unusual formats). This is the standard hybrid pattern. D and B use an agent for the whole flow even though it is deterministic, which is costly and unpredictable. C crams everything into one prompt. Remember: deterministic parts = workflow; agents only at decision points.

questions.question: A teammate has asked you to explain why the team's Claude application is billed for output tokens at a different rate than input tokens. They had assumed the rate was the same for both. How would you explain the difference?

options.text: Output tokens are typically billed at a higher rate than input tokens, and cost models for the application should reflect both rates separately.
Output tokens are not billed at all, because cost is determined entirely by the input tokens sent to the model on each request.
Output tokens are typically billed at the same rate as input tokens, and the apparent rate difference is a billing error to report to Anthropic.
Output tokens are typically billed at a lower rate than input tokens, because output tokens are cheaper to produce than input tokens are to process.

questions.explanation: Output tokens are usually priced higher than input tokens, so the cost model must keep the two prices separate. B (output not billed), C (equal prices, a billing error) and D (output cheaper) all get the direction wrong. Remember: output tokens cost more than input tokens.

questions.question: Your Claude application runs long agentic workflows where the agent makes many tool calls, and the conversation history grows quickly. After about 20 tool calls, you notice the agent's responses become less focused and sometimes ignore earlier task constraints. How would you address this?

options.text: Apply context engineering techniques such as tool output pruning or compaction to keep the active task state visible while reducing the volume of older content.
Restart the agent every five tool calls to prevent any drift, with the agent losing all task state at each restart point during the workflow.
Increase the model's context window so the agent can hold every tool output at full detail across the entire workflow no matter how many tool calls it accumulates.
Remove tool calling from the workflow entirely so the agent operates as a single textgeneration step with no tool outputs accumulating in the context window.

questions.explanation: Context bloat from accumulated tool output calls for tool output pruning or compaction: keep the active task state and reduce the volume of old content. C enlarging the context window does not fix buried information; B restarting loses state; D dropping tool calling drops the capability itself. Remember: accumulated tool output = pruning / compaction.

questions.question: Your team's Claude agent has accumulated several customizations that bypass the SDK's defaults, including custom history management, retry logic, and error handling. A new team member has proposed reverting all the customizations to maintain the codebase more easily. The tech lead disagrees and says each customization was added for a reason. How would you advise the team?

options.text: Decide on each customization individually based on its original reason and the SDK's current capabilities.
Keep all customizations, trusting that the tech lead's original reasoning is still valid.
Migrate the agent off the SDK and rebuild it with a custom loop.
Revert all customizations to the SDK's defaults to standardize the codebase.

questions.explanation: Each customization was added for a reason, but the SDK's capabilities have changed, so review each customization against its original reason and the current SDK. B and D are the two extremes, keep everything or remove everything; C abandoning the SDK and rebuilding is an unnecessary escalation. Remember: judge each one by its original reason + current SDK capabilities.

questions.question: A teammate has asked you to explain the difference between context engineering and prompt engineering. They have heard the terms used interchangeably and are unsure how each applies to a Claude application that processes long-running multi-step tasks. How would you describe the distinction?

options.text: Prompt engineering is the older term for prompt design, while context engineering is the newer term that has replaced it in modern Claude applications across the industry.
Prompt engineering shapes individual prompts for specific outputs, while context engineering manages how content flows across turns and steps and takes steps to keep relevant state visible.
Prompt engineering and context engineering each address content the team gives Claude, but the team can group them under a single workflow because the practices use overlapping techniques.
Prompt engineering focuses on the model's response, while context engineering focuses on the user's input across many sessions in a long-running multi-step Claude application.

questions.explanation: Prompt engineering shapes an individual prompt for a specific output; context engineering manages the flow of content across turns and steps so the relevant state stays visible. A treats it as a renaming; C merges the two concepts; D defines both wrongly (response vs input). Remember: prompt = one turn; context = across turns and steps.

questions.question: You are extending a Claude agent with a capability that needs to be reusable across multiple teams in the organization, with each team able to invoke and use it independently. How would you build the capability?

options.text: As a custom tool embedded in this team's agent only, with other teams able to copy the implementation into their own agents when they need the capability.
As a Skill or MCP server because both are purpose-built for cross-team reuse independently by each consuming team.
As a wrapper around an existing built-in tool that adds the missing functionality, on the grounds that built-in tools cover the reuse pattern when extended carefully.
As a shared library that each team imports into its own Claude application code, with each team responsible for keeping the library up to date in its integration.

questions.explanation: Reuse across many teams, each calling it independently, is exactly what a Skill or an MCP server is designed for. A and D make each team copy code or maintain its own library, which causes drift. C wrapping a built-in tool does not solve reuse. Remember: cross-team reuse = Skill or MCP server.

questions.question: Your Claude application is hitting context window limits when processing long customer service transcripts. A junior developer suggests increasing the temperature parameter to fix the issue. How would you respond?

options.text: Increase the temperature parameter as the junior developer suggested and observe whether the context window issue resolves over the next several runs of the application in production.

Adjust the temperature parameter together with the max_tokens parameter, treating the combined adjustment as the team's mechanism for managing context window pressure during long-transcript processing.
Remove the system prompt entirely to make room for longer transcripts in each request, freeing up context window space the system prompt would otherwise consume.
Explain that temperature controls sampling randomness and is unrelated to context capacity, then address the context issue through summarization or chunking.

questions.explanation: Temperature controls randomness in sampling and has nothing to do with context capacity, so correct the misconception and handle it with summarization or chunking. This question duplicates Q22 with the letters swapped (D here, B in Q22). Learn the content, not the letter. Remember: temperature ≠ context capacity → summarize/chunk.

questions.question: Your Claude application is hitting context window limits when processing long customer service transcripts. A junior developer suggests increasing the temperature parameter to fix the issue. How would you respond?

options.text: Adjust the temperature parameter together with the max_tokens parameter, treating the combined adjustment as the team's mechanism for managing context window pressure during long-transcript processing.
Explain that temperature controls sampling randomness and is unrelated to context capacity, then address the context issue through summarization or chunking.
Remove the system prompt entirely to make room for longer transcripts in each request, freeing up context window space the system prompt would otherwise consume.
Increase the temperature parameter as the junior developer suggested and observe whether the context window issue resolves over the next several runs of the application in production.

questions.explanation: Same as Q21: temperature is a sampling parameter, not context capacity; handle it with summarization or chunking. The clearest evidence that the source sets swap letters between practice sets: the same question has answer B here and D in Q21. Remember: temperature ≠ context capacity → summarize/chunk.

questions.question: You are building a Claude application that needs to deliver model output to end users as it is generated, instead of waiting for the full response to complete. The Claude API mechanism you would use is...

options.text: Structured JSON output, which delivers responses only after the model has finalized the JSON shape across the entire response.
Streaming responses, which deliver tokens incrementally as the model generates them so users see output progressively.
Prompt caching, which speeds up the cost profile of future requests and does not affect the delivery timing of the first response.
The Batch API, which delivers full responses after a delay suitable for non-interactive workloads.

questions.explanation: Output has to reach the user while it is being generated, so use a streaming response that returns tokens incrementally. D (Batch API) is the opposite on latency; C (prompt caching) affects cost, not how output is delivered. Remember: progressive display = streaming; long wait, non-interactive = Batch.

questions.question: Your Claude application processes 50-page legal contracts and produces summaries with citation references back to the source. The team is debating whether to send each contract whole or split it into smaller pieces. The contracts fit within Claude's context window. Initial testing shows that whole-document processing produces summaries with stronger cross-section reasoning but occasionally drifts on citation accuracy in later sections. Chunked processing produces stronger citation accuracy per chunk but loses cross-section reasoning. The team has not decided which property matters more. How would you guide the team's decision?

options.text: Identify which property matters more for the application's actual use case and let that decision drive the chunking approach, then validate the choice against representative contracts.
Assess the cost and latency implications of both approaches against the application's performance requirements before recommending which processing strategy to adopt.
Review the citation accuracy results from chunked processing and determine whether the loss of cross- section reasoning produces summaries that still meet the application's quality bar.

Examine the use cases where cross-section reasoning failures occur and assess whether whole- document processing meets the application's accuracy requirements across a representative sample of contracts.

questions.explanation: The question says the team has not yet decided which attribute matters more, so the job is to establish the actual use-case requirements, let them drive the choice, and validate on representative contracts. B, C and D are all reasonable analyses but skip the real bottleneck: nobody has settled which criterion takes priority. Remember: no priority criteria yet → define requirements first, then validate.

questions.question: Your team is choosing how to add a capability to a Claude application. You want to apply the appropriate option, whether built-in tool, custom tool, Skill, or MCP server, based on the use case. You would choose the option that...

options.text: Is the newest available option among built-in tools, custom tools, Skills, and MCP servers.
Matches the use case's scope, reuse needs, and integration context.
Is the easiest to build given the team's current development tools and workflows.
Is the most familiar to the team based on prior experience with similar capabilities.

questions.explanation: Choose an extension mechanism by the use case's scope, reuse needs and integration context, not by novelty, ease or familiarity. A, C and D are all criteria about the development team rather than the problem. Remember: choose by scope + reuse + integration context.

questions.question: You are designing a Claude application that will require structured JSON output for downstream processing. The output schema is well-defined, and downstream systems will reject malformed JSON.

options.text: Define a clear schema, structure the prompt to request output in that schema, and validate Claude's output against the schema before passing it downstream.
Structure the prompt to request output in a schema that is described in plain English, with downstream systems parsing whatever shape Claude produces.
Avoid structured output and use free-form text everywhere instead, on the grounds that free-form text is more flexible and handles edge cases better than structured schemas.
Define a clear schema and structure the prompt to request output in that schema, with downstream systems handling any validation needed.

questions.explanation: Downstream rejects malformed JSON, so do all three: define a clear schema, have the prompt require that schema, and validate before passing output downstream. D is like A but pushes validation downstream, missing exactly the key step. B describes the schema in prose. Remember: clear schema + prompt to the schema + validate before downstream.

questions.question: Your Claude application receives untrusted input from external sources. The team is establishing how the application should treat this untrusted input. Untrusted input would be...

options.text: Routed through a separate Claude application with more lax security controls so the original application does not handle the untrusted input directly.
Treated identically to trusted input from internal sources, on the grounds that all input the application receives can be handled the same way.
Validated and sanitized before being incorporated into prompts, and treated as data the model should not interpret as instructions.
Blocked entirely so the application accepts only trusted input, with no path for legitimate external input the application might process.

questions.explanation: Untrusted input must be validated and sanitized before going into the prompt, and treated as data rather than instructions for the model to execute. B treats all input the same; D blocks everything and loses legitimate use cases; A moving to a 'looser' app is a security paradox. Remember: untrusted input = validate/sanitize + treat as data, not commands.

questions.question: You are establishing the guardrail strategy for a Claude application. The team wants to ensure guardrail failure does not expose the application to unsafe behavior. The guardrail strategy would...

options.text: Apply guardrails at the model level only and rely on the model's built-in safety behaviors to handle any cases the guardrail does not explicitly cover.
Apply guardrails at the application output level only and route flagged responses to a human reviewer before they are delivered to the user.
Layer multiple guardrails so a single guardrail failure does not expose the application to unsafe behavior.
Implement a single comprehensive system prompt guardrail and validate its coverage against the application's full range of expected inputs.

questions.explanation: The requirement says one failed guardrail must not expose the system, so layer several guardrails (defense in depth). A, B and D are each a single layer (model level only, output level only, one system prompt), which is exactly what the question wants to avoid. Remember: one guardrail failing must not expose the system ⇒ layered guardrails.

questions.question: A teammate has asked you to explain why your Claude agent's tools include detailed descriptions in the tool definition, even when the tool name is already descriptive. The teammate suggests removing the descriptions to simplify the tool definitions. How would you respond?

options.text: Suggest moving the descriptions out of the tool definition and into a separate documentation file the team maintains so the tool definitions stay short and the descriptions remain available.
Explain that the model uses the tool description to decide when to call the tool, and descriptions disambiguate cases where the tool name is not enough.
Agree with the teammate because tool names are sufficient for the model to choose the right tool on every request the agent handles.
Suggest replacing the descriptions with example calls embedded in the tool definition, treating example calls as a complete substitute for the prose description.

questions.explanation: The model uses the tool description itself to decide when to call a tool; the description distinguishes cases the tool name alone cannot. A moves the description into a separate documentation file, taking it out of the model's view. D treats example calls as a full replacement for the description. Remember: tool description = the signal the model uses to choose tools.

questions.question: You are building an agent that needs to call several internal APIs and a database in a structured, repeatable way. Your team has decided to use the Claude Agent SDK rather than build a custom loop. You are setting up the agent's tool definitions and execution loop. How would you set up the tools and execution loop?

options.text: Call the Messages API directly and let the model format its tool calls in plain text.
Use the SDK's tool interface and loop, with conversation history stored in a separate team database.
Use the SDK's tool interface and write the loop and history layer in the team's own code.
Use the SDK's tool interface and let the SDK handle the loop, dispatch, and history.

questions.explanation: The team has decided to use the Agent SDK instead of writing its own loop, so use the SDK's tool interface and let the SDK handle the loop, dispatch and history. B and C still rewrite what the SDK already does, contradicting the decision. A drops structured tool calling. Remember: once you choose the SDK, use its loop, dispatch and history.

questions.question: Your Claude application's error handling currently logs every API error with the same severity level. The team wants to differentiate between errors that should page an on-call engineer and errors that should be logged for later review. How would you structure the error handling?

options.text: Page on every error, on the grounds that paging guarantees that no error is missed by the team during normal operation across the application's lifecycle.
Log every error with the same severity, on the grounds that differentiating severity adds complexity that does not pay off in most application setups over time.
Categorize errors by severity based on impact and recoverability, then route each category to the appropriate channel for paging or logging.
Disable logging for any error that does not page, treating non-paging errors as not worth recording for later review either.

questions.explanation: Classify errors by severity based on impact and recoverability, then route each class to the right channel (page or log). A paging on every error causes alert fatigue; B keeps the status quo; D stops logging errors that do not page. Remember: severity by impact + recoverability, then routing.

questions.question: A team has deployed a multi-agent system in which a primary agent decomposes user requests and delegates subtasks to three specialized subagents: one for data retrieval, one for analysis, and one for report generation. In production, the team observes that subagents are making redundant tool calls, occasionally exceeding token budgets, and sometimes producing outputs that contradict each other - all of which the primary agent passes along without catching. What is the most appropriate way to address these failures?

options.text: Collapse the three subagents into a single large-context model call that handles retrieval, analysis, and generation in one pass.

Add retry logic to each subagent so that when a tool call fails, the subagent retries automatically before escalating - and configure each subagent to log its tool calls and outputs to a shared trace so the team can audit redundancy and contradictions after the fact.
Give each subagent read access to the other subagents' outputs so they can identify and resolve contradictions without routing back through the primary agent.

Strengthen the primary agent's management layer to enforce per-subagent tool budgets, validate outputs against a defined schema before passing them forward, and establish explicit handoff contracts between stages.

questions.explanation: The three symptoms (duplicate tool calls, exceeded token budget, self-contradicting output) are failures of the management layer, so tighten the primary agent: a token budget per subagent, schema validation of outputs before handing them on, and explicit handoff contracts between stages. B only adds retries and tracing, detecting problems after the fact without preventing them. C lets subagents read each other, losing isolation with nobody to arbitrate. A tears down the architecture. Remember: coordination failures → tighten the management layer: budget + schema + handoff contract.

questions.question: The Anthropic API deprecated a request parameter that your Claude application uses in approximately 40 places across the codebase. The deprecation notice gives a six-month window before the parameter is removed and recommends a replacement parameter with slightly different semantics. You would respond to the deprecation by...

options.text: Swapping all 40 call sites in a single change right away to prevent drawn-out migration work that will delay ongoing functioning.
Keeping the deprecated parameter in place while writing a wrapper function around it to insulate the rest of the codebase from the eventual change.
Migrating all 40 call sites in a single change near the removal date to ensure the deprecated parameter continues to work as long as possible.
Adding regression tests to cover the parameter's behavior, then migrating call sites in batches that you validate against regression tests.

questions.explanation: With six months and slightly changed semantics, add regression tests covering the parameter's behavior, then migrate in batches and re-verify after each batch. A and C are both 'big bang' moves (immediately or right before the deadline) with no safety net; B wraps the call but keeps the soon-to-be-removed parameter. Remember: deprecation = regression tests first, migrate in batches.

questions.question: You are setting up a Claude application that will run a mix of multi-turn conversations and one-off requests. You want to use caching techniques to reduce token costs where they apply. A teammate suggests caching the model's output as well, so the application does not have to make duplicate Claude calls when similar queries arrive. You would apply prompt caching to...

options.text: Nothing, because prompt caching does not affect cost in any application that mixes multiturn conversations and one-off requests in a single deployment.
Only the user's input portion of each request because user input is the part of the prompt that varies the most across the application's normal operation.
The static portions of prompts that are repeated across requests, such as system prompts, instructions, or shared context.
The model's output, treating the response from each request as cacheable content the application can return on similar future queries.

questions.explanation: Prompt caching applies to the static parts repeated across requests: the system prompt, instructions and shared context. D is the colleague's mistaken proposal itself: prompt caching does not cache model output. B caching the most variable part is pointless. Remember: cache the repeated static part, not the output.

questions.question: A Claude application that worked well in testing is now occasionally returning outputs that mention information not present in the input. The development team initially assumed the model was hallucinating, so they asked you to troubleshoot. What would you do first?

options.text: Apply a retrieval-augmented generation pattern to ground the responses in source content before any further investigation of the production traces.
Replace the current model with a larger one to reduce the chance of hallucination, on the grounds that larger models tend to hallucinate less in typical applications.
Add a system prompt instruction telling the model not to invent information, on the grounds that prompt-level instructions are the fastest fix for hallucination concerns.
Examine production traces to identify whether the issue is hallucination by the model, context loss, prompt injection, or another failure mode before recommending a fix.

questions.explanation: The team has assumed it is hallucination. The first step is to look at production traces to determine whether it really is hallucination, context loss, prompt injection or another failure mode: diagnose before prescribing. A, B and C are all fixes for a single assumption that has not been verified. Remember: don't trust the assumption — classify the failure mode from traces first.

questions.question: Your Claude application's prompt was written months ago and has not been updated. The team has discovered through evals that the prompt produces good results on common cases but underperforms on a specific category of inputs that has grown in volume. How would you respond?

options.text: Replace the prompt with a new one aligned to the underperforming category, treating any common-case performance change as a known tradeoff.
Add the underperforming category to a separate Claude application with its own prompt so the original prompt does not change.
Iterate on the prompt to address the underperforming category, validate the change with evals, and continue refining as needed.
Tell users to avoid the underperforming category by adding warnings in the application's user interface about handled inputs.

questions.explanation: Iterate on the prompt to handle the weak input group, verify the change with evals, and keep refining: a measured improvement cycle. A trades away performance on normal cases; B splits into a separate app, fragmenting the system; D pushes the problem onto users. Remember: prompt improvement = iterate + validate with evals.

questions.question: Your Claude agent performs database operations. A recent incident occurred where the agent ran a destructive query that affected production data. The team wants to add deterministic controls to prevent similar incidents. How would you prevent similar incidents?

options.text: Switch to a higher-capability Claude model on the grounds that a more capable model is less likely to run destructive queries during normal operation across all requests.
Run the agent only during business hours when humans are available to monitor its activity, treating the schedule as the primary control mechanism for destructive operations.
Add Claude hooks that intercept database operations and apply deterministic checks, such as blocking destructive queries or requiring approval, before the queries execute.
Add a system prompt instruction telling the agent to be careful with database operations on every request the application handles during normal operation across all incoming traffic.

questions.explanation: The question asks for a deterministic control, so use Claude hooks to intercept database operations and apply deterministic checks (block destructive queries or require approval) before the query runs. D relies on prompt instructions, which are not deterministic. A changes the model and B limits working hours: neither is a technical control. Remember: deterministic control = hooks that intercept before execution.

questions.question: Your team uses several plugins across multiple Claude applications, and a recent plugin update introduced a regression. The team had not been tracking plugin versions, so the team cannot easily identify which version was previously working. How would you address this?

options.text: Add explicit plugin version tracking to the project's configuration so the team can identify, pin, and upgrade plugin versions deliberately.
Treat plugins as untrackable third-party code and rely on plugin authors to communicate breaking changes when they happen, with no internal version tracking.
Upgrade every plugin to the latest version on a regular cadence to keep version drift small, on the grounds that drift contributes to regression risk.
Stop using all plugins until the team can rebuild equivalent functionality directly into the application code, treating plugin avoidance as a way to remove version-related risk.

questions.explanation: The cause is that plugin versions are not tracked, so add explicit version tracking to the project configuration so versions can be identified, pinned and upgraded deliberately. B leaves it to the plugin authors; C upgrading continuously does not tell you which version used to work; D dropping the plugin is an overreaction. Remember: plugin regression = version tracking + pinning.

questions.question: You are designing an agent that handles a complex claim-processing workflow. Each claim moves through fact extraction, eligibility evaluation, and a decision step. The three subtasks have distinct success criteria, and some claims require iteration between fact extraction and eligibility evaluation before a decision can be reached. Which agent pattern would you apply?

options.text: A single tool-use loop pattern that gives one agent access to all the tools needed for fact extraction, eligibility evaluation, and decision-making.
A streaming pattern that emits partial decisions as the agent processes each claim, refining the output until a final decision emerges from the stream.
A graph-based pattern that lets the agent move between subtasks based on the state of each claim, with each subtask evaluated against its own criteria.
A linear chain pattern that processes every claim through fact extraction, then eligibility evaluation, then decision, with no return paths between subtasks.

questions.explanation: There are three subtasks with their own criteria and a need to go back between steps, so use a graph-based pattern that moves between subtasks according to each claim's state. D is a linear chain with no way back, directly contradicting the iteration requirement. A puts every tool into one loop and loses each step's criteria. Remember: need loops between steps = graph-based, not a linear chain.

questions.question: Your team is debating how to manage the prompts used in your Claude application. Some prompts are checked into the code repository, some live in a separate configuration file, and some are constructed inline at runtime. The result is inconsistent, and a recent prompt change went out without code review. What steps would you take?

options.text: Establish a single source of truth for prompts, version-control them alongside code, and require code review for prompt changes.
Move all prompts out of version control to a separate spreadsheet that team members can edit freely as the application evolves over time.
Establish a single source of truth for prompts but keep change review optional, allowing developers to update prompts directly when changes are urgent.
Move all prompts to inline runtime construction so the team can update them quickly through a streamlined process outside the standard code review workflow.

questions.explanation: Prompts are artifacts that affect production behavior, so keep a single source of truth under version control with the code and require code review for changes. C is like A but makes review optional, which is exactly the failure the question describes (changes going out without review). B and D lose control entirely. Remember: prompt = code: single source of truth + version control + review.

questions.question: Your agent is processing tasks that take 30 to 60 minutes to complete. Each task has welldefined intermediate checkpoints, and the team wants the agent to be able to resume from the most recent checkpoint if a process is interrupted. How would you implement this resumability?

options.text: Apply a checkpointing pattern that persists the agent's intermediate state and reloads that state when resuming an interrupted task.
Run two copies of the agent in parallel for every task and use whichever one finishes first as the source of truth.
Restart the task from the beginning whenever a process is interrupted.
Increase the agent's timeout to several hours so that interruptions become rare enough to ignore in practice.

questions.explanation: A 30–60 minute task with well-defined checkpoints calls for a checkpointing pattern: persist intermediate state durably and reload it on resume. C restarting from scratch ignores the requirement; D raising the timeout does not handle interruptions; B running two copies in parallel doubles the cost. Remember: resume = checkpointing (persist + reload state).

questions.question: You are implementing a custom tool for your Claude agent. The tool needs to interact with an external pricing service that returns product data. Which of the following best practices would you apply as you develop this tool?

options.text: Omit the tool description and let the model infer when to use the tool based on the tool's name and the rest of the prompt context.
Implement the tool with no error handling and let the agent loop catch failures whenever the pricing service returns an error during operation.
Define the tool with a loose schema and let the model interpret the inputs flexibly on each call the agent makes.
Define the tool with a clear schema, write a precise description for when to call it, and handle pricing service errors explicitly.

questions.explanation: Three best practices for custom tools: a clear schema, a precise description of when to call the tool, and explicit handling of external service errors. A, B and C each drop exactly one of those three (no description, no error handling, a loose schema). Remember: custom tool = clear schema + when-to-call description + error handling.

questions.question: Your Claude application's token costs have grown faster than expected. The team has not been tracking token usage by feature, so the team cannot identify which features are driving cost. The team is debating how to respond. How would you respond?

options.text: Tell the team that cost growth is unavoidable as the application scales and that no investigation will change the trajectory of the application's cost over the next several quarters.
Add token usage tracking by feature to the application's logging so the team can identify which features drive cost before recommending changes.
Switch every feature to the smallest model to cut cost broadly across the application during normal operation.
Reduce token usage uniformly across all features by half, applying the cut evenly across the application during normal operation.

questions.explanation: You cannot fix the right place without knowing which feature burns the cost, so add per-feature token usage tracking to logging before recommending changes. C and D cut across the board without measuring; A gives up. The principle: measure first, cut second. Remember: don't cut before measuring — instrument per feature first.

questions.question: Your Claude application's content policy specifies categories of content it should not produce under any circumstance. The application currently has no mechanism to enforce this policy, and content matching these categories is appearing in the application's output. How would you enforce the content policy?

options.text: Remove the content policy entirely and let any output reach users during normal operation, accepting whatever content the application produces in response to incoming traffic.
Add deterministic output filtering that checks responses against the content policy before they reach users.
Move enforcement to users by asking them to report content policy violations after the violating content has already reached them in the application's responses.

Enhance the system prompt to contain explicit instructions for the categories to avoid, complete with examples of each category. Treat the strengthened prompt as the primary enforcement mechanism for the application's content policy across all responses.

questions.explanation: The content policy has categories that must never be generated, so use deterministic output filtering that checks responses against the policy before they reach users. D sounds convincing (a detailed prompt with examples) but still treats the prompt as the primary enforcement mechanism, which a prompt is not. C leaves detection to users after the fact. Remember: 'never' = deterministic output filter, not a prompt.

questions.question: A new agent your team built handles customer support tickets, but it routinely gets confused when a single ticket spans billing, shipping, and product issues. The agent often loses track of which sub-issue it has already addressed and revisits the same one. The team is considering architectural changes. What architectural change would you recommend?

options.text: Add detailed prompting that instructs the agent to track which sub-issues have been resolved and which remain.
Increase the size of the agent's context window so it can hold the full ticket history at once .
Switch to a deterministic workflow that handles billing, shipping, and product issues in a fixed sequence.
Introduce an orchestrator agent that delegates billing, shipping, and product sub-issues to dedicated subagents.

questions.explanation: One ticket spans several areas and the agent loses track of which have been handled, so an orchestrator delegates each area to a specialized subagent with its own state. A uses prompting to 'remind the agent to keep track', which is not an architectural change. B forces a fixed order and loses flexibility. C enlarging the context window does not fix lost state. Same content as Q95 (letters swapped). Remember: one request, many areas = orchestrator + a subagent per area.

questions.question: You are building a Claude application that needs to maintain a persistent connection to a service that streams real-time updates. The team is unsure what communication pattern to use. Which communication pattern would you use?

options.text: A single long HTTP request the server holds open indefinitely, with no standard WebSocket framing on the connection.
A WebSocket, because WebSockets are designed for bidirectional, persistent, real-time communication between the client and the streaming service.
File-based communication where the service writes new updates to disk and the application polls the file system for changes.
Repeated short-lived HTTP polling requests, where the application opens a new HTTP connection each time it checks for updates.

questions.explanation: A persistent, bidirectional, real-time connection is exactly what WebSocket is designed for. A (long-poll held open indefinitely), C (via files) and D (constant short polling) all avoid WebSocket and are all worse at the stated requirement. Remember: persistent + bidirectional + real-time = WebSocket.

questions.question: Your Claude application requests structured JSON output from the model. Most of the time the JSON is well- formed, but occasionally Claude returns malformed JSON that breaks downstream processing. How would you handle the malformed output?

options.text: Manually inspect every response before downstream processing so a human reviewer catches any malformed JSON before the application passes the response to downstream systems.
Switch to free-form text output so the application no longer depends on JSON parsing for any of the responses it sends to downstream systems during normal operation.
Add output validation that parses Claude's response against the expected schema and treats malformed output as a recognized error path with retry or fallback handling.
Retry the same request repeatedly until valid JSON appears in the model's response, with the retry loop adding delay to the application's response time on affected requests.

questions.explanation: Add output validation that parses responses against the expected schema and treats malformed output as a recognized error path with retry or fallback. D just retries blindly until it gets lucky; A puts a person into every request; B drops JSON altogether. Remember: malformed JSON = validate + recognized error path (retry/fallback).

questions.question: Your Claude application is producing inconsistent outputs for similar inputs, even when using the same model and prompt. You want to debug the issue systematically. Your debugging approach would...

options.text: Capture full traces of input, system prompt, user messages, model output, and parameters, then analyze the differences between consistent and inconsistent runs.
Retry every request that produces an unexpected output and log the results to identify whether repeated calls converge on a consistent response pattern.
Assume inconsistent outputs reflect normal LLM non-determinism and document the variability as an accepted characteristic of the application's behavior.
Lower the model's temperature and re-run the inconsistent inputs to determine whether the parameter change reduces output variability across runs.

questions.explanation: Systematic debugging means capturing full traces (input, system prompt, user message, output, parameters) and comparing consistent runs with inconsistent ones. D lowering temperature tries a fix before understanding the problem; B retrying and logging does not isolate variables; C accepts it and closes the case. Remember: debugging = full traces + compare good vs bad runs.

questions.question: Your agent makes 10 to 15 tool calls per task, and you have noticed it sometimes loses track of earlier results by the time it reaches later steps. The agent's context window is large enough to hold all the messages, but the relevant information appears to get buried as the conversation grows. How would you address this?

options.text: Switch to a different agentic framework that advertises automatic context-window management as a built-in feature.
Reduce the number of tool calls per task by combining several existing tools into larger, multi-purpose tools.
Apply a context-management pattern that summarizes or prunes older tool outputs while preserving the active task state.
Increase the context window further so all tool outputs from every prior step remain in full detail throughout the task.

questions.explanation: The context window is large enough but information gets buried, so use a context-management pattern: summarize or prune old tool output while keeping the active task state. D enlarging the window makes the burying worse (the question says the window is big enough). B merging tools into a multipurpose tool lowers tool-selection accuracy. A switches frameworks. Remember: buried information ≠ lack of space → summarize/prune, keep active state.

questions.question: You are deciding between Claude models for a task. The team has identified three relevant tradeoff dimensions: quality, latency, and cost. The right model is the one that...

options.text: Meets the task's quality requirements at an acceptable latency, with cost reviewed separately once the quality and latency bar has been established.
Fits the task's quality, latency, and cost requirements together, recognizing that improving one dimension typically affects the others.
Satisfies the task's latency requirement first, then is evaluated against quality and cost thresholds to confirm the selection is acceptable across all three dimensions.
Meets the task's cost target within a defined latency budget, with quality validated against a representative sample of inputs after the model is selected.

questions.explanation: Quality, latency and cost have to be considered together because improving one usually affects the others. A, C and D all work sequentially, fixing one dimension before looking at the others, which is the 'separate trade-offs' trap. Remember: weigh all three together, not one after another.

questions.question: A Claude application is producing outputs that drift away from the expected JSON format after several conversation turns. The first few turns produce correctly formatted output, but later turns gradually lose structure. How would you address the drift?

options.text: Truncate every response to the first few characters, validate that the truncated output matches the expected JSON structure, and log any mismatches for review.
Switch to a smaller Claude model and re-test the application to determine whether the drift persists across conversation turns.
Identify the failure mode as format drift, examine how the conversation context evolves over turns, and address the drift through context management or output validation.
Restart the application after every turn and monitor whether the format remains consistent across subsequent interactions.

questions.explanation: The right process: identify the failure mode as format drift → examine how the context evolves across turns → address it with context management or output validation. A truncating responses and validating the truncated part is pointless; B switching to a smaller model is unrelated to the cause; D restarting every turn abandons the multi-turn conversation. Remember: format drift = diagnose the context + context management/validation.

questions.question: You are explaining to a stakeholder why running the same Claude prompt twice can produce slightly different results. The stakeholder is concerned this means the application is broken. How would you address the stakeholder's concern?

options.text: Tell the stakeholder the variation is a bug that the team will fix in the next release of the application, then create a work ticket to fix the bug.
Tell the stakeholder the variation comes from network latency and that switching to a faster network connection will produce more consistent results across runs.
Tell the stakeholder the variation is caused by Claude being updated continuously by Anthropic, and that switching to a fixed model snapshot will eliminate the variation entirely.
Explain that LLMs are non-deterministic by default due to sampling, and describe how the application handles this through validation, retries, or temperature adjustment.

questions.explanation: LLMs are non-deterministic by default because of sampling; explain that and describe how the application handles it (validation, retries, temperature tuning). A calls it a bug; B blames network latency; C blames continuous Anthropic updates and promises a fixed snapshot will eliminate all variation (not true). Remember: non-determinism from sampling + how the application handles it.

questions.question: You are setting up the configuration management approach for a new Claude Code project. Your team will use CLAUDE.md files and settings.json files to control behavior, and you want to make sure changes are tracked and reviewable. The configuration management approach would...

options.text: Version-control CLAUDE.md and settings.json files alongside the project's source code, with changes reviewed through standard pull request workflows the team applies.
Version-control CLAUDE.md and settings.json files in a separate repository from the project's source code, so configuration evolves independently from the application code over time.
Duplicate CLAUDE.md and settings.json files in multiple repositories to provide redundancy, on the grounds that a single source of truth is risky for project configuration.
Version-control CLAUDE.md alongside the project's source code and settings.json files in a separate repository from the project's source code.

questions.explanation: CLAUDE.md and settings.json are project configuration, so version-control them with the source code and route changes through standard pull request review. B and D move the configuration to another repo, losing its link to the code; C copies it to many places, breaking the single source of truth. Remember: Claude Code config = version control with the code + PR review.

questions.question: Your Claude application is deployed to development, staging, and production environments. Each environment uses a different model version, different prompt versions, and different plugin dependencies, but the configuration is currently scattered across environment variables, hardcoded values, and undocumented setup scripts. How would you manage the configuration?

options.text: Use the latest available model version everywhere and stop pinning model versions, on the grounds that pinning adds maintenance overhead the team should aim to reduce.
Standardize all environments to use the same configuration values to eliminate the differences between development, staging, and production.
Consolidate the configuration into a version-controlled system documenting model version pinning, prompt versioning, and plugin dependencies for each environment.
Move all configuration into hardcoded application code to reduce reliance on external configuration sources that are difficult to track over time.

questions.explanation: The three environments legitimately differ, so consolidate configuration into one version-controlled system and document the pinned model version, prompt version and plugin dependencies for each environment. B forcing the three environments to be identical defeats the purpose of staging and dev; A drops version pinning; D hardcodes it in code. Remember: multiple environments = version-controlled config, pinned per environment.

questions.question: You are writing a system prompt for a Claude application that needs to produce output in a specific JSON shape. The downstream system will reject any output that does not match the schema. Your prompt would need to...

options.text: Instruct Claude to return JSON sometimes and free text other times so the application's output captures both formats.
Omit any reference to the format and rely on a post-processing step in the application to reshape Claude's output.
Include explicit constraints describing the required JSON schema and an instruction to produce only output matching that schema.
Instruct Claude to use whichever output format it considers most appropriate for each request the application handles.

questions.explanation: Downstream rejects any output that deviates from the schema, so the prompt must state the JSON schema constraints explicitly and instruct the model to produce only output matching that schema. B relies on post-processing; A and D let the model choose the format. Remember: the prompt must state the schema explicitly + 'output only to the schema'.

questions.question: Your team is preparing to roll out a configuration change that updates several prompt versions across a Claude application used by multiple downstream systems. The change has already been tested in staging, but the team has not assessed how the prompt change will affect each downstream system that depends on the application's output. What would you do before rolling out the change?

options.text: Document the prompt version changes in the application changelog and proceed with the rollout, treating the staging test results as sufficient evidence of impact across all downstream systems.
Notify downstream system owners that a change is coming and schedule the rollout for the following week, without conducting a formal impact assessment.
Assess the configuration impact on each downstream system before rolling out, and coordinate with downstream system owners as needed.
Limit the rollout to systems that were explicitly included in staging testing, and defer all other downstream systems until a later release cycle.

questions.explanation: The team has not assessed the impact on each downstream system, so assess the configuration's impact on each system before rollout and coordinate with the downstream owners. A treats staging results as enough; B only notifies without assessing; D limits the rollout but still does not assess the impact. Remember: a prompt change affecting many consumers = impact assessment first.

questions.question: A teammate has submitted a pull request that adds a Claude-powered feature to your service. The code works, but the prompt and model selection are hard-coded inline, error handling is missing, and there are no tests for the integration. What would you request during code review?

options.text: Approve the pull request as-is, on the grounds that the feature works in the happy path and the missing pieces can be added in follow-up commits.
Approve the pull request and add the missing pieces yourself in a follow-up commit so the teammate can move on to other work immediately.
Request changes that move prompt and model configuration to a configurable location, add error handling for Claude API failures, and add tests for the integration.
Request changes that move prompt and model configuration to a configurable location and add tests, treating the missing error handling as a follow-up release item.

questions.explanation: The question lists three gaps: hardcoded prompt/model, no error handling and no tests, so request changes for all three. D is like C but defers error handling to a later release, deliberately dropping one of the three. A and B both approve. Remember: three gaps means requesting fixes for all three, deferring none.

questions.question: Your team uses Claude Code across multiple repositories. You want the team's rules and general coding standards to apply to all repositories, and other rules to apply only to specific repositories. The team is currently duplicating instructions across every repository's CLAUDE.md file. How would you address this?

options.text: Stop using CLAUDE.md altogether and ask each developer to configure Claude Code manually for each project they work on.
Use a single repository's CLAUDE.md as the central source of truth and link to it from every other repository's CLAUDE.md file.
Use a CLAUDE.md hierarchy that scopes general standards broadly and project-specific context within each repository's local CLAUDE.md.
Move all instructions to a separate documentation site that developers consult during Claude Code sessions across all repositories.

questions.explanation: Use the CLAUDE.md hierarchy: shared standards scoped at a broad level, and each project's specific context in that repo's local CLAUDE.md. B uses one repo as the source and links to it from others, which is still manual duplication, not the hierarchy mechanism. A and D drop CLAUDE.md. Remember: shared standards + per-repo context = CLAUDE.md hierarchy.

questions.question: A teammate has asked how the Claude SDK handles transient API errors, such as a temporary network issue or a brief rate-limit response. They want to know whether the application code needs to handle every transient error or whether the SDK provides any default behavior. How would you describe the SDK's default behavior?

options.text: The SDK provides default retry behavior for network errors but surfaces rate-limit responses directly to the application code, which must implement its own retry logic for those cases.
The SDK provides default retry behavior for transient errors up to a fixed number of attempts, and this behavior is not configurable.
The SDK provides default retry behavior for many transient errors, and the application code can configure or extend that behavior as needed.
The SDK logs transient errors to a default error stream and continues execution without retrying, leaving the application code responsible for detecting and responding to failed calls.

questions.explanation: The SDK retries many transient errors by default, and the application can configure or extend that behavior (for example max_retries). B says it cannot be configured; A says rate-limit errors are not retried; D says the SDK just logs and continues. Remember: SDK: default retries + configurable.

questions.question: The product team has described a new Claude feature in business terms: "agents should help our analysts produce client memos faster." You need to convert this into actionable technical requirements for the engineering team. Your first step would be to...

options.text: Assess what similar agent-based features have been built internally or in the industry and use those precedents to scope the technical approach.
Ask the analysts about the current memo production process to see where they think Claude could be introduced as a prompt-driven drafting step.
Examine what model capabilities and tier options are available and determine which best supports the memo drafting workflow described by the product team.
Interpret the functional and infrastructure requirements implied by the business goal.

questions.explanation: The task is to translate a business goal into technical requirements, so the first step is to interpret the functional and infrastructure requirements the goal implies. A relies on precedent and C jumps to choosing a model tier, both before any requirements exist. B (asking the analysts) is a reasonable discovery activity and a secondary candidate, but D answers the question actually being asked. Remember: business goal → interpret functional + infrastructure requirements.

questions.question: Your Claude agent's hooks are currently triggered for every action, which slows down the agent significantly even when actions pose no risk. The team wants to scope hooks more carefully. How would you scope the hooks?

options.text: Disable the agent during peak hours so the hook overhead does not slow the application down during the busiest periods of the day across the application's operation.
Disable all hooks while the team re-scopes them, treating the period of no hook enforcement as a temporary state during the re-scoping work.
Scope hooks to only the high-risk actions, such as destructive operations or sensitive data access, and remove hooks from low-risk actions to balance safety with performance.
Replace hooks with system prompt instructions on the grounds that prompt instructions can produce the same enforcement effect that hooks produce on the agent's actions.

questions.explanation: Scope hooks to the high-risk actions (destructive operations, access to sensitive data) and remove them from low-risk actions, balancing safety with performance. B disabling every hook creates an unprotected window; D replacing hooks with prompt instructions loses determinism; A turns the agent off by schedule. Remember: hooks only on high-risk actions.

questions.question: Your Claude application produces good responses for typical inputs but struggles with edge cases. You have several labeled examples of edge-case inputs and the desired response for each. You want to use these examples to improve the model's handling of edge cases. What is the best way to use these examples?

options.text: Train a custom model on the edge-case examples and deploy that custom model in place of the team's current Claude integration.
Add the labeled edge-case examples to the prompt as few-shot examples so the model can learn the pattern.
Tell users to avoid submitting the edge-case inputs to the application by adding warnings in the application's user interface.
Embed the examples in a database for the model to find during inference.

questions.explanation: Labeled examples of the edge cases are available, so put them in the prompt as few-shot examples so the model picks up the pattern. A training a custom model is a big escalation (and Claude is not fine-tuned this way in this context); D embeds them in a database without saying how they are used at inference; C pushes it onto users. Remember: labeled examples available = few-shot in the prompt.
