questions.question: You are building a Claude application that processes 10,000 customer emails overnight to extract structured data. The work is non-interactive, runs once daily, and has a flexible completion window of several hours. Which Claude API would you use?

options.text: The real-time Messages API with concurrent requests to process the emails as fast as possible during the overnight window.
The Batch API, which is designed for non-interactive workloads with flexible completion windows.
The streaming responses API to process each email and return partial results to a database as the model generates them.
The real-time Messages API, processing the emails one at a time sequentially to ensure consistent ordering of results.

questions.explanation: Non-interactive, run once a day, with a flexible completion window of several hours: that is exactly the Batch API's use case. A and D use the real-time Messages API for work that does not need real time (more expensive); C uses streaming when nobody is watching. Remember: non-interactive + flexible window = Batch API.

questions.question: Your Claude application's outputs are inconsistent in format. The team's instructions are scattered across the system prompt and user messages, with some instructions stated only once and others repeated. How would you fix the inconsistency?

options.text: Move all instructions into the user message so the application's behavior is controlled at the input point.
Place each instruction wherever the developer who first wrote it found most natural, retaining the original intent.
Repeat all instructions in both the system prompt and the user message so the model sees each instruction more than once.
Consolidate behavioral and format instructions in the system prompt and keep user messages focused on the user's input.

questions.explanation: Consolidate behavior and formatting instructions in the system prompt, and keep the user message to the user's input only. A does the opposite (everything in the user message); C repeats them in both places, creating conflicting sources; B keeps the inconsistency. Remember: behavior/format in the system prompt; the user message is just input.

questions.question: You are setting up Claude Code for a new project repository. Your team has shared coding standards, preferred libraries, and project-specific context that every developer working on the repository should have available when they use Claude Code. How would you set this up?

options.text: Document the standards in a separate wiki page maintained outside the repository so the documentation stays decoupled from the source code.
Add the coding standards and project context to the repository's existing README file and direct developers to reference it when starting Claude Code sessions.
Configure Claude Code through environment variables that each developer sets on their own machine when they begin working in the repository.
Initialize Claude Code in the repository and document the standards and project-specific context in a CLAUDE.md file at the repository root.

questions.explanation: Coding standards, preferred libraries and project context must be available to every developer using Claude Code, so initialize Claude Code in the repo and document them in CLAUDE.md at the repo root. A and B put them in a wiki or README, which Claude Code does not load as context automatically; C uses per-machine environment variables, causing drift. Remember: shared project context = CLAUDE.md at the repo root.

questions.question: You are integrating Claude into an application written in Python. The Claude SDK provides a Python client that wraps the underlying REST API. How would you integrate the SDK?

options.text: Use the Claude Python SDK and let it handle authentication, retries, and response parsing through its standard documented patterns for Python integrations.
Use a different LLM provider's SDK and translate the responses into Claude's API shape so the application can switch providers in the future.
Skip the SDK and embed Claude calls in shell commands invoked from Python, so that the application runs the calls outside the main Python process.
Call the REST API directly with raw HTTP requests so the application avoids the SDK's abstraction between the application code and the API.

questions.explanation: Use the Claude Python SDK itself and let it handle authentication, retries and response parsing following the documented standard patterns. D calling raw REST rewrites what the SDK already does; C calling through the shell is odd; B uses another provider's SDK and translates. Remember: if there is an official SDK, use it.

questions.question: The team is debating whether to build a new capability as a custom tool or to use an existing built-in tool that nearly covers the use case but lacks one specific feature. How would you decide?

options.text: Examine the custom tool option by scoping the implementation effort and determining whether the additional flexibility justifies the development and maintenance cost.
Identify whether the team has previously built similar custom tools and use those precedents to determine which approach is more consistent with the existing codebase.
Evaluate whether the missing feature can be addressed by extending the built-in tool or warrants a custom tool, then choose accordingly.
Review the built-in tool's documentation and assess whether its existing capabilities are sufficient to cover the use case without any modification or extension.

questions.explanation: Assess whether the missing functionality can be covered by extending a built-in tool or truly needs a custom tool, then choose accordingly. A considers only one branch (custom tool); D only the other (built-in as is); B chooses by internal precedent. Only C compares both branches, as the question asks. Remember: compare extending built-in vs custom, then choose.

questions.question: Your Claude application uses structured output that is consumed by downstream code. The team wants to handle malformed or unexpected output gracefully so it does not crash downstream systems. The best choice for handling this issue would be to...

options.text: Apply defensive parsing to handle unexpected fields, missing values, and type mismatches that the downstream code might otherwise crash on.
Crash on any unexpected output and require manual recovery on affected requests the application handles during normal operation.
Use the output the model produces and leave schema enforcement to a later phase of production after the application is more complete.
Silently drop any output that does not match expectations so downstream systems do not see the malformed output the application receives from the model.

questions.explanation: Defensive parsing: handle unexpected fields, missing values and wrong types — exactly the three things that crash downstream code. D silently dropping output loses data without a trace; B crashes and recovers manually; C postpones schema enforcement. Remember: safe downstream = defensive parsing (extra/missing/wrong type).

questions.question: You are configuring Claude Code for a new project. The team needs to set permissions, default model selections, and environment-specific behavior at the project level so the configuration is consistent across all developers working on the repository. The Claude Code mechanism you would use is...

options.text: A system prompt embedded in every Claude Code conversation by each developer at the start of every session in the project.
The settings.json file, scoped at the project level so the configuration applies consistently across developers and persists with the repository.
A shared spreadsheet that lists configuration values for team members to reference and update by hand as the project evolves.
Environment variables that each developer sets on their own machine when working with Claude Code on the project.

questions.explanation: Permissions, the default model and environment-specific behavior are needed at project level, consistent for every developer, so use a project-scoped settings.json that travels with the repository. A relies on each developer pasting a system prompt; C uses a spreadsheet; D uses per-machine environment variables — none are consistent or travel with the repo. Remember: project-level configuration = settings.json (project scope).

questions.question: The Claude application your team built has grown over six months, and the prompt-handling code has accumulated duplication and tangled control flow. The functionality is working, but new features are getting harder to add. How would you address this?

options.text: Continue adding features and plan a refactoring pass after the next two release cycles when the team has more bandwidth for internal work.
Refactor the prompt-handling code in small increments as part of each new feature ticket, treating the cleanup as a side effect of feature work.
Move all the prompt-handling code into a single large function to reduce the number of files developers have to navigate when reading the code.
Plan a refactoring pass to consolidate duplicated logic, separate concerns, and simplify control flow before adding new features.

questions.explanation: Technical debt has made adding features progressively harder, so plan a refactor that consolidates duplicated logic, separates responsibilities and simplifies control flow before adding new features. B refactoring 'alongside' each feature ticket sounds reasonable but does not fix control flow tangled across modules; A postpones for two cycles; C merging into one big function makes it worse. Remember: features getting harder to add = refactor first, don't pile on.

questions.question: You are building an MCP server that exposes several internal data sources as MCP resources. The server needs to be deployed so multiple Claude applications can integrate with it. How would you approach the build and deployment?

options.text: Deploy the MCP server only on individual developer machines, with the Claude applications unable to reach the server outside each developer's machine.
Author the server with clearly defined resources, tools, and prompts, choose a communication pattern, and deploy to an accessible hosting environment.
Build the MCP server with resource and tool definitions scoped to the first Claude application that needs it, and extend the definitions to additional applications as each integration is requested.
Bypass the MCP server and embed each data source directly in every Claude application that needs the data, with each application maintaining its own integration.

questions.explanation: Do all three: clearly define the resources, tools and prompts, choose the communication pattern, and deploy to a hosting environment many applications can reach. A deploys only on a developer's machine; C scopes it to the first application and expands later (drift); D drops MCP and embeds directly into each app. Remember: shared MCP = clear definitions + chosen transport + reachable hosting.

questions.question: You are deciding between deploying a Claude-powered agent on Anthropic's hosted infrastructure or self- hosting under a "bring your own cloud" model in your own AWS account. The agent processes customer data subject to your enterprise's data residency policies, but the team wants to ship quickly and avoid managing infrastructure. Which deployment model would you recommend?

options.text: Deploying on Anthropic-hosted infrastructure while the team drafts a request to update the enterprise data residency policy to accommodate hosted AI deployments.
Self-hosting under BYOC to satisfy the data residency requirement, while working with the infrastructure team to reduce the operational overhead of managing the deployment.
Self-hosting under BYOC for an initial pilot, then evaluating whether to migrate to Anthropic-hosted infrastructure once the agent's data-handling patterns are better understood.
Deploying on Anthropic-hosted infrastructure to meet the team's shipping timeline, and flagging the data residency requirement for a follow-up compliance review after launch.

questions.explanation: Data residency is a mandatory constraint, so self-host with BYOC to satisfy it, while working with the infrastructure team to reduce the operational burden. A hard constraint beats the wish to ship fast. A and D both ship first and handle compliance later; C pilots on BYOC but leaves moving to hosted open, still not treating the constraint as a condition. Remember: data residency = hard constraint → BYOC, reduce overhead afterwards.

questions.question: You maintain a Claude application that uses Claude Sonnet 4.5 across several production workflows. Anthropic released Claude Sonnet 4.7, which your evaluation suite shows performing 8% better on your highest-volume task. However, this version produces different output formatting on two of your structured- extraction prompts that downstream consumers parse with regex-based code. To roll out the upgrade, you would...

options.text: Keep the older model in production to preserve the fragile parsing layer that may risk breaking with any model change.
Adjust the prompts to constrain output format, re-run evaluations against the expected parsing-layer schema, then roll the model out with a feature flag and the option to revert per workflow.
Rewrite the downstream parsing code to accept a wider range of output formats to ensure the application is resilient to future model upgrades without requiring prompt changes.
Switch the model identifier in the application's configuration to the new model, then monitor production for parsing failures to be fixed as failures surface.

questions.explanation: The full rollout process: adjust the prompt to constrain the format → re-run evals against the schema the parsing layer expects → roll out behind a feature flag with a per-workflow revert path. D changes the model identifier and 'waits for errors to surface' in production; A freezes permanently; C only fixes the parsing layer without addressing the format cause. Remember: upgrade = adapt prompt + re-eval + feature flag + revert path.

questions.question: Your Claude agent has too many tools, and many of them have overlapping functionality. The agent often picks an inappropriate tool when several could plausibly handle a request. How would you address the tool selection problem?

options.text: Remove all tools and rely on the agent's general capability instead, with the application losing the workflows that previously relied on tools.
Restructure the tool set by consolidating overlapping tools, removing unused tools, and clarifying tool descriptions so each tool has a distinct purpose.
Add more tools to cover every variation of the requests the agent handles, on the grounds that more tools give the agent more accurate options to choose from.
Add detailed examples to each tool's description so the agent can match incoming requests to the right tool by example, treating the examples as the team's selection mechanism.

questions.explanation: Restructure the tool set: merge overlapping tools, remove unused ones and clarify descriptions so each tool has a distinct purpose. C adding a tool for every variant makes it worse; D only adds examples while keeping the overlap; A removes every tool. Remember: wrong tool choice = merge/remove/clarify descriptions.

questions.question: Your enterprise has a contract with AWS that requires Claude API calls to flow through Amazon Bedrock rather than the direct Anthropic API. Your team is building a new Claude application and is unfamiliar with this constraint. How would you build the application?

options.text: Configure the application to invoke Claude through the Bedrock-compatible API path while keeping the application's logic provider-agnostic.
Build the application against the direct Anthropic API and ignore the contractual requirement to route Claude calls through Amazon Bedrock.
Build the application against the direct Anthropic API now and migrate to Bedrock in a follow-up release once the team has more experience with the Bedrock API.
Build two parallel implementations of every call, one for the direct Anthropic API and one for Bedrock, and pick the faster one at runtime.

questions.explanation: The contract requires going through Bedrock, so configure the application to call Claude through the Bedrock-compatible API path while keeping the application logic provider-agnostic. B ignores the contractual constraint; C postpones it to a later release; D builds two parallel implementations. Remember: contractual constraint = comply now + keep code provider-agnostic.

questions.question: You are designing a Claude application that processes user-submitted text. Some of that text could include sensitive information such as account numbers or passwords that the application should not send to Claude. How would you design the application?

options.text: Log all user-submitted text before it is sent to Claude and review the logs periodically to identify whether sensitive information is reaching the model.
Add a prompt instruction in the system prompt specifying the categories of sensitive information Claude should disregard when processing user-submitted text.
Apply filtering at the boundary for the most commonly observed sensitive data patterns and expand coverage to additional patterns based on findings from production monitoring.
Define the application boundary explicitly, identify what content can leave the boundary for Claude, and add filtering or redaction at the boundary.

questions.explanation: Explicitly define the application boundary, decide what content may leave it to reach Claude, and add filtering/redaction at the boundary. C filters only 'common' patterns and expands based on production, letting sensitive data through first and learning later. B uses prompt instructions (the data has already reached the model). A only logs for later review. Remember: sensitive data = define the boundary + redact at the boundary.

questions.question: Your application uses the Messages API to handle multi-turn conversations. Each new turn resends the entire conversation history, and your token costs are growing as conversations get longer. You suspect there is a more efficient approach. How would you address this?

options.text: Switch to the Batch API for every turn so the per-call cost is reduced, treating the batch as the team's primary cost-control mechanism for multi-turn work.
Truncate every conversation to the last two messages so that token usage stays low and costs remain predictable across the application's normal operation.
Summarize each conversation after every turn and replace the full history with the summary on the next request, reducing token count at the cost of fidelity.
Use prompt caching to reuse the static portions of the conversation context across turns instead of paying for them at the normal input-token rate on every request the application sends.

questions.explanation: Each turn resends the whole history, so use prompt caching to reuse the static part of the conversation context across turns instead of paying the normal input-token price for it on every request. B trimming to the last two messages and C summarizing after each turn both sacrifice accuracy (the question says a more efficient option exists); A uses the Batch API for an interactive conversation. Remember: resending multi-turn history = prompt caching of the static part.

questions.question: The team is debating whether to integrate with the Claude API directly or through a thirdparty abstraction layer that supports multiple LLM providers. The team has identified that all current and projected use cases run on Claude, no internal customer has requested LLM portability, and the team's product roadmap does not mention multi-provider support over the next two years. The third-party abstraction would add roughly 15 percent overhead in code complexity and introduce one additional dependency. Which integration approach would you recommend?

options.text: A custom multi-provider abstraction layer the team builds in-house so that the team controls every part of the abstraction the application uses for its API calls.
Direct integration with Claude through its SDK, because no multi-provider need exists and abstraction would add complexity that does not pay off.
The third-party abstraction layer, on the grounds that multi-provider support is valuable for any application as a matter of long-term flexibility across vendors.
Both integration paths in parallel, where the application uses each path on different runs to compare which performs better in production over time.

questions.explanation: The question lists the evidence: every use case runs on Claude, nobody requires portability, the two-year roadmap has no multi-provider plans, and the abstraction adds 15% complexity, so integrate directly through the SDK. C argues 'long-term flexibility is always worth it' despite the contrary evidence; A builds its own abstraction; D runs two paths in parallel. Remember: no real need, no added abstraction.

questions.question: Your team's Claude application has been in production for a year, and the team has decided to formalize its testing strategy. Currently, the team writes ad-hoc tests for individual features but has no overall testing approach. What testing approach would you formalize?

options.text: Define unit tests for individual functions, integration tests for the Claude integration, and end-to-end tests for critical user flows, applied consistently across the codebase.
Define a single testing approach that uses end-to-end tests and apply it consistently across all new features as they are added to the codebase.
Continue writing ad-hoc tests as features ship and introduce a peer review step to ensure each test adequately covers the feature being released.
Adopt a test-driven development practice where unit tests are written before each feature is implemented and must pass before code is merged.

questions.explanation: A complete test strategy has several layers: unit tests for individual functions, integration tests for the Claude integration, and end-to-end tests for critical user flows, applied consistently. B uses only one layer (end-to-end); C stays ad hoc; D is about TDD (a test-writing process), not the structure of the test strategy. Remember: test strategy = unit + integration + e2e, consistently.

questions.question: Your Claude application returns confident-sounding answers, but occasionally those answers contain factual errors that downstream systems treat as ground truth. The team is concerned about the application's confidence-versus-accuracy gap. How would you address the gap?

options.text: Add a disclaimer to every output telling users to verify the accuracy of the output and treat the disclaimer as the primary mechanism for managing the confidence-versus-accuracy gap.
Reject every response the application produces until a manual accuracy review is conducted on each response by a human reviewer before any downstream system uses it.
Lower the model's temperature so the model's responses sound less confident and downstream systems are less likely to treat the responses as ground truth in normal operation.
Apply skepticism toward confident output by adding validation steps, sourcing requirements, or confidence calibration before treating outputs as ground truth.

questions.explanation: The gap between 'sounds confident' and 'is actually correct' needs verification mechanisms: a validation step, required sourcing, or confidence calibration, before treating output as ground truth. A uses a disclaimer as the main mechanism; C lowers temperature so it 'sounds less confident' (accuracy does not change); B makes people review every response. Remember: confident ≠ correct → validation + sourcing + calibration.

questions.question: You are designing a Claude application that maintains user sessions across multi-turn conversations. The product team has asked how the application will handle session lifecycle: when sessions should expire, how state is reset, and how the application avoids carrying stale context into new conversations. How would you design session lifecycle?

options.text: Define a single short session timeout that applies across all conversations and treat the timeout as the application's complete session lifecycle mechanism.
Define state reset triggers tied to specific application events but apply them across all sessions globally, with no per-session expiration rules.
Define explicit session expiration rules, state reset triggers, and rules for starting fresh sessions so stale context does not leak into new conversations.
Define explicit session expiration rules but rely on users to start new conversations when they want fresh context, with no automatic reset triggers in the application.

questions.explanation: A complete session lifecycle means explicit expiration rules, state-reset triggers and fresh-start rules, so old context does not leak into new conversations. A has only a timeout; B has reset triggers but no expiration; D has expiration but leaves resetting to users. Each wrong answer lacks exactly one component. Remember: session lifecycle = expiration + reset triggers + fresh-start rules.

questions.question: You are designing an agent that handles a multi-step research task. You want the agent to break the task into smaller pieces, hand each piece to a focused subagent, and consolidate the results. The agent pattern you would apply is...

options.text: A memory pattern that stores the entire research history in advance, before any subtask begins execution.
A single tool-use loop that includes every tool the agent might need across all subtasks.
An orchestrator and subagent pattern with specialized subagents assigned to each subtask.
A context-window pruning pattern that drops each subtask's content after the agent moves on.

questions.explanation: Splitting the task into smaller parts, assigning each to a focused subagent, then merging the results is exactly the orchestrator and subagent pattern. B, one loop holding every tool, is the opposite of specialization; A and D are context/memory management techniques, not task-decomposition patterns. Remember: decompose + delegate to subagents + merge = orchestrator pattern.

questions.question: The product team has asked you to choose a Claude model for a new feature. The team has provided functional requirements but has not specified performance, cost, or quality targets. The team's product manager says, "Use whatever model gives us the best results." How would you respond?

options.text: Choose a mid-tier model and ship the feature, because mid-tier models work for most use cases without specified targets.
Ask the product team to specify quality, latency, and cost targets, then select the model whose tradeoffs best fit those targets.
Choose the largest, highest-capability Claude model, on the grounds that "best results" is most likely to mean highest quality.
Run every Claude model on a representative sample and pick whichever scores best on a generic benchmark.

questions.explanation: You cannot choose a model without targets, so ask the product team to state the quality, latency and cost targets, then choose the model whose trade-offs fit best. A, C and D all pick a model based on guesses about what 'best results' means or on a generic benchmark not tied to the use case. Remember: missing targets = clarify them first, don't guess.

questions.question: A teammate has asked you to explain when a Skill would be the right choice over an MCP server. The teammate is unsure how the two differ in practice when both can be reused across teams. How would you explain the distinction?

options.text: A Skill bundles prompts, scripts, and data into a package the model loads as a unit while an MCP server exposes resources, tools, and prompts through a standard client interface.
A Skill is preferable for cross-team reuse because it loads more efficiently than an MCP server during normal operation in the team's typical multi-team workloads.
A Skill and an MCP server are equivalent extension mechanisms that the team can use interchangeably for any reusable capability that needs to be accessible across teams.
A Skill is the older mechanism and an MCP server is the newer one, so the team should prefer an MCP server for any reusable capability that the team builds going forward.

questions.explanation: A Skill packages prompts, scripts and data into a bundle the model loads as a unit; an MCP server exposes resources, tools and prompts through a standard client interface. B compares them by 'loads more efficiently' (not the distinguishing point); C says they are equivalent; D says old versus new. Remember: Skill = package the model loads; MCP = standard interface exposing resources/tools.

questions.question: Your Claude agent has access to a tool that retrieves customer records. A teammate has noticed that the agent occasionally calls the tool with arguments the schema does not declare, and the tool's downstream service returns an error each time. The teammate proposes loosening the schema so the tool accepts whatever arguments the model produces. How would you respond?

options.text: Add a system prompt instruction telling the model to produce schema-conforming arguments, treating the prompt instruction as the primary mechanism for keeping the agent's tool calls valid.
Remove the schema entirely and rely on the downstream service to reject invalid calls, treating the downstream service as the team's primary enforcement layer.
Loosen the schema as the teammate proposed so the downstream service receives every call the agent makes during normal operation.
Keep the schema strict, validate arguments before dispatching, and return a structured error so the agent can retry.

questions.explanation: Keep the schema strict, validate parameters before dispatch, and return structured errors so the agent can retry on its own — a proper feedback loop. C is the colleague's mistaken proposal itself (loosening the schema); B drops the schema and relies on downstream; A uses prompt instructions as the main mechanism. Remember: bad tool arguments = strict schema + validation + structured error for retry.

questions.question: Your Claude application's API keys are stored in a secrets manager. The team is debating whether the same key should be used in development, staging, and production environments. How would you handle the keys across environments?

options.text: Use a single development key everywhere on the grounds that production keys are too risky to deploy across the application's three environments during normal operation.
Use distinct keys for each environment so a compromise in one environment does not affect the others during normal operation across the application's lifecycle.
Use the same key across all environments for simplicity and treat the propagation of any compromise as a known operational tradeoff for the team's key management approach.
Rotate the same key across environments at random intervals on the grounds that random rotation provides isolation between environments without requiring distinct keys.

questions.explanation: Use a separate key for each environment so a compromise in one environment does not spread to the others. A and C share one key and treat the spread as a 'known trade-off'; D rotating the same key at random intervals creates no isolation at all. Remember: one key per environment (blast radius).

questions.question: Your Claude application uses tool calling to fetch patient data and generate summary reports. The flow occasionally fails because the model returns a tool_use block that references arguments not present in the schema, and your application code does not handle this case gracefully. How would you address this?

options.text: Retry the same request repeatedly until the model returns a valid tool_use block that matches the schema as expected.
Validate the tool_use block's arguments against the tool schema before dispatching the tool and handle invalid arguments as a recognized error path.
Log invalid tool_use blocks when they occur and allow the tool dispatch to proceed, relying on the tool's own error handling to surface failures back to the application.
Stop using tool calling entirely and replace tools with prompted text generation that asks the model to describe what it would do.

questions.explanation: Validate the parameters in the tool_use block against the tool schema before dispatch, and treat invalid parameters as a recognized error path. C only logs and still dispatches; A retries blindly; D drops tool calling. Same principle as Q85, but this question asks about the application-code side. Remember: validate tool_use arguments before dispatch, treat errors as an error path.

questions.question: You have just shipped a new Claude-powered application to production. The development phase is complete, and the system is now in active use by internal teams. The next phase of work for this system is...

options.text: Operating and maintaining the system, including monitoring, responding to issues, and planning evolution.
Handing the system over to a separate operations team that will manage it independently of the development team going forward.
Running a formal post-deployment review that assesses the development phase before the team does any further work on the system.
Retiring the system, since shipping is the final lifecycle stage for any application that reaches production.

questions.explanation: After shipping, the next phase is operation and maintenance: monitoring, incident response and planning the evolution. D says shipping is the last phase (wrong about the lifecycle); B hands everything to an independent ops team; C makes the post-deployment review a blocker for everything else. Remember: after shipping = operate & maintain (monitor, respond, evolve).

questions.question: You are setting up a CI/CD pipeline for a new Claude application. The pipeline needs to run automated checks on every pull request before code can be merged. The CI/CD checks would include...

options.text: Automated linting and security scanning, with Claude integration testing handled manually during pre- release verification by a designated reviewer.
Automated tests of the Claude integration, linting, and any other standard quality gates the team applies to its other services.
Automated tests of the Claude integration only, with linting handled separately during local development on each developer's machine.
A full end-to-end production deployment on every pull request to catch all possible issues before any code is merged into the main branch.

questions.explanation: CI must automatically run the tests for the Claude integration, linting, and the standard quality gates the team applies to its other services. A pushes integration tests to manual checks; C drops linting from CI; D deploys to production on every pull request. Remember: CI = Claude integration tests + linting + standard quality gates.

questions.question: You are starting a new Claude application and have a small set of well-labeled examples that demonstrate the desired output format. You want to use these examples to guide Claude's behavior. How would you guide the application's behavior?

options.text: Train a custom model on the labeled examples before deployment so that the application does not need to include the examples in any prompt during operation.
Use zero-shot prompting and rely on the model's general capability to produce the desired output format consistently across all incoming requests.
Embed the examples in a database and retrieve them at runtime as reference material for the team.
Use multi-shot prompting by including the labeled examples in the prompt so Claude can match the desired output format on each request.

questions.explanation: A good set of labeled examples of the desired format already exists, so use multi-shot prompting: put the examples in the prompt so Claude matches the format on each request. B uses zero-shot despite having good examples; A trains a separate model; C stores them in a database as 'reference material for the team' instead of putting them in the prompt. Remember: labeled examples available = multi-shot in the prompt.

questions.question: Your Claude application has multi-step workflows where each step's output is needed only briefly before the agent moves on. The cumulative tool output is filling the context window with content that is no longer relevant. How would you handle the accumulating tool output?

options.text: Keep every tool output in the context indefinitely so the agent has the full record of every step it has executed during the workflow.
Switch to a smaller Claude model that processes context more efficiently and treat any quality loss as a tradeoff for the cost reduction.
Apply prompt caching to the accumulated tool outputs so the application does not re-pay for the older content on each subsequent step.
Apply tool output pruning to remove tool outputs that are no longer needed by later steps in the workflow.

questions.explanation: Each step's output is needed only briefly, so use tool output pruning: remove tool outputs that later steps no longer need. C uses prompt caching for accumulated content — caching lowers cost but does not free the context window. A keeps everything; B switches to a smaller model. Remember: output no longer needed = pruning (caching does not free context).

questions.question: A teammate has asked how to extend Claude Code with a custom Skill that the team can invoke during sessions. The Skill consists of a set of instructions and a few support scripts the team wants Claude to be able to call when the Skill is loaded. Where is the right place to define the Skill?

options.text: Define the Skill in a personal scratch directory on each developer's machine and load it manually before each Claude Code session that needs it.
Define the Skill in a Skills directory recognized by Claude Code, where Claude can discover and load it during sessions for the team's repositories.
Define the Skill inside the application's source code as a regular library module and call it from the application code instead of from Claude Code.
Define the Skill as a long inline instruction at the top of every CLAUDE.md file in the team's repositories so Claude has access to it on every session.

questions.explanation: Define the Skill in a Skills directory that Claude Code recognizes, so Claude discovers and loads it automatically in sessions for the team's repository. A keeps it in a personal scratch directory and loads it manually; C turns the Skill into a library called from application code (the wrong consumer); D inlines it into every CLAUDE.md. Remember: Skill = a Skills directory Claude Code recognizes.

questions.question: A Claude application is occasionally refusing to answer questions that should be in scope, including questions the application has answered correctly in the past. You want to investigate. What is the first step of your investigation?

options.text: Examine traces of the refused requests to identify what triggers the refusal, whether input patterns, system prompt content, or other context.
Assess whether the refusals cluster around specific input patterns, question types, or time periods by analyzing the distribution of refused requests in the logs.
Identify which questions have been refused and compare them against previously answered questions to determine what changed between the successful and refused interactions.
Test whether removing or adjusting those instructions resolves the behavior.

questions.explanation: The first step is to look at traces of the refused requests to determine what triggers the refusals: input patterns, system prompt content or other context. It is the broadest step and assumes no cause in advance. B and C are narrower analyses based on logs or comparisons, i.e. steps that come after you have traces; D jumps straight to trying a fix ('those instructions') before knowing which instructions. Remember: the first step is always to look at traces, before fixing anything.

questions.question: A teammate is reviewing the team's threat model for a Claude application and has asked you to identify the categories of AI-specific threats that the model should cover. The teammate has already listed traditional web application threats and wants to know what additional categories apply to a Claude application. Which AI-specific threat categories would you add?

options.text: Cross-site scripting and SQL injection, because these traditional web application threats apply with equal weight to any application that uses Claude in any way.
Prompt injection, data leakage from prompts or context, jailbreak attempts, and unsafe model output that bypasses application controls.
Network-level denial of service and physical infrastructure attacks, because these categories cover the threats most likely to affect any Claude application in production.
Supply chain attacks on the Claude SDK because the SDK itself is the only point of vulnerability that a Claude application introduces beyond traditional web application threats.

questions.explanation: The four AI-specific threat categories: prompt injection, data leakage from prompts or context, jailbreaks, and unsafe output that bypasses the application's controls. A and C list traditional web and infrastructure threats (which the colleague already has); D narrows it to a single point, the SDK supply chain. Remember: AI threats = injection + data leakage + jailbreak + unsafe output.

questions.question: A new agent your team built handles customer support tickets, but it routinely gets confused when a single ticket spans billing, shipping, and product issues. The agent often loses track of which sub-issue it has already addressed and revisits the same one. The team is considering architectural changes. What architectural change would you recommend?

options.text: Introduce an orchestrator agent that delegates billing, shipping, and product sub-issues to dedicated subagents.
Switch to a deterministic workflow that handles billing, shipping, and product issues in a fixed sequence.
Add detailed prompting that instructs the agent to track which sub-issues have been resolved and which remain.
Increase the size of the agent's context window so it can hold the full ticket history at once.

questions.explanation: Same as Q45: one ticket spans several areas and the agent loses track of state, so an orchestrator delegates to specialized subagents per area. This is the duplicate of Q45 with the letters swapped (D in Q45 → A here), which is exactly why you should learn the content and not the letter. Remember: one request, many areas = orchestrator + a subagent per area.

questions.question: Your team is integrating Claude into an existing REST API service. The service handles concurrent requests, and you are deciding how to structure the Claude API calls within the existing async codebase. How would you structure the Claude calls?

options.text: Use the Claude SDK's async client and structure Claude calls as awaitable operations alongside the rest of the service's async code.
Replace the existing async REST service with a synchronous service to match the call style of synchronous Claude SDK clients.
Run Claude API calls in a separate thread pool isolated from the rest of the service so the main event loop is not affected.
Make synchronous Claude API calls and block the async event loop until each call completes before processing the next request.

questions.explanation: The service is already async and handles requests concurrently, so use the Claude SDK's async client and write Claude calls as awaitable operations that fit the rest of the async code. D blocks the event loop; B converts the whole service to synchronous; C pushing calls to a separate thread pool is needless complexity when an async client exists. Remember: async codebase = async client + await.

questions.question: Your team is preparing a new Claude application for production, and the product team has asked for a cost projection. The team needs to estimate the cost based on expected request volume, average input length, and average output length. How would you build the projection?

options.text: Build a cost model based on expected request volume and the chosen model's pricing, treating average input and output token counts as variables to be estimated post-launch.
Build a cost model that uses the average per-request cost from a similar Claude application the team built last year, scaling that figure by expected request volume.
Build a cost model that combines expected request volume and average input tokens, treating output tokens as a small enough share of cost to leave out of the projection.
Build a cost model that combines expected request volume, average input tokens, average output tokens, the chosen model's pricing, and any caching benefits.

questions.explanation: A complete cost model includes request volume, average input tokens, average output tokens, the chosen model's prices, and the savings from caching. C leaves out output tokens; A treats input/output as variables to estimate after launch; B extrapolates from a different, older application. Remember: cost model = volume × (input + output tokens) × model price − caching.
